overview: The exact atlas record represents Late and Final Jomon archaeology, not a state, nation, language, or single people. Its 1500 to 323 BCE lifetime overlaps conventional phase labels, but those labels and dates vary across Japan. Communities lived in pit dwellings, gathered and managed plants, hunted, fished, stored food, made pottery and lacquerware, exchanged valued materials, buried their dead, and built communal places. Northern wetland preservation reveals wooden and lacquered objects that dry sites lose; shell middens preserve food and human remains while leaving other routines obscure. Four of five atlas snapshots repeat a three-part polygon from Kyushu through northern Honshu, then the 400 BCE file transfers western probes to Yayoi while retaining an eastern and northern component. That software seam is useful to audit but cannot date migration or cultural replacement. No securely attributable Late or Final Jomon writing survives, so the card provides an explicit absence instead of inventing a sample. Around 300 BCE, rice farming and Yayoi material spread unevenly; Epi-Jomon and other regional histories continued. The ending is transformation, interaction, and changing archaeological labels.

periods.title: 1500 to 1350 BCE: regional Late Jomon chronologies begin
periods.summary: Late Jomon phase boundaries differ among ceramic regions and radiocarbon sequences. Okyozuka illustrates why local dates must be tested rather than copied nationwide. This first teaching slice marks an approximate analytical opening, not a founding event, migration date, or moment when every community changed together.

periods.title: 1350 to 1200 BCE: storage strategies remain local
periods.summary: Storage pits varied in number and capacity through time and between settlements. Such differences may reflect foods, seasonality, household choices, or preservation. They warn against turning one excavated pit pattern into a universal Late Jomon economy, even when communities across several regions practiced planned storage.

periods.title: 1200 to 1050 BCE: Kiusu receives communal earthworks
periods.summary: Around 1200 BCE, people at Kiusu built large circular burial earthworks, gateways, graves, and standing stones. Moving an estimated three thousand cubic meters of soil shows sustained coordination. The site documents collective labor in Hokkaido, not a capital directing every Late or Final Jomon community.

periods.title: 1050 to 900 BCE: stone settings and gathering places
periods.summary: At Omori Katsuyama, a large oval stone circle dating near 1000 BCE stood with pits, hearths, dumps, and ritual stone objects. Its long axis aligns toward the winter-solstice sunset. The association supports repeated gathering and ceremony while leaving leadership, calendar rules, and participants unnamed.

periods.title: 900 to 750 BCE: populations follow different paths
periods.summary: Paleodemographic estimates suggest that Kanto, Aomori, and Hokkaido did not share one population curve. Decline in one region could accompany stability or growth elsewhere. Sampling and preservation limit precision, but the contrast firmly resists a single nationwide story of Late Jomon demographic collapse.

periods.title: 750 to 600 BCE: wet places preserve exceptional craft
periods.summary: Kamegaoka wetland deposits preserve lacquered pottery, wooden objects, plant materials, jade, figurines, and other items rarely surviving on dry sites. Nearby graves show a substantial cemetery. Preservation creates an unusually rich view, so its material abundance should not automatically define every Final Jomon settlement.

periods.title: 600 to 450 BCE: cultivation and gathering coexist
periods.summary: Plant management and cultivation developed through locally different histories. Archaeobotanical evidence supports active husbandry in eastern Japan without making all Jomon households full-time farmers. Gathered nuts, cultivated plants, fishing, and hunting could coexist, and their proportions changed with region, season, and chronology.

periods.title: 450 to 300 BCE: rice farming spreads unevenly
periods.summary: Rice agriculture expanded discontinuously rather than crossing the archipelago in one wave. Western communities encountered new crops and material practices earlier than many eastern and northern groups. The interval closes an archaeological teaching frame while interaction, ancestry, and diverse regional traditions continued beyond it.

sections.title: Read the atlas as evidence about the atlas

items.text: The exact id is late-jomon-culture, indexed as an approximate culture from 1500 to 323 BCE. It has no summary, card, override, or staged draft. This packet preserves that database identity while proposing a separately reviewed name and chronology for a more accurate public card.

All fifty border snapshots were decoded. The target is absent at 2000 BCE, then appears exactly once in five files: 1500, 1000, 700, 500, and 400 BCE. Coverage metadata matches those intervals, and no target feature falls outside the indexed lifetime. That verifies bookkeeping, not archaeological borders.

From 1500 through 500 BCE, one MultiPolygon repeats unchanged: three components, 246 positions, and bounds near 129.34 to 142.00 east and 30.89 to 41.44 north. Tested points from Kagoshima to Kamegaoka fall inside, while Sapporo, Okinawa, and Busan remain outside.

At 400 BCE, the target shrinks to one polygon covering tested points from Yoshigo and Nagano through Kanto, Sendai, and northern Tohoku. Kyoto, Tsukumo, Shikoku, Fukuoka, and Kagoshima repaint to Yayoi. One shared TopoJSON arc records that edit, not a precisely dated ethnic frontier.

The target disappears in the 323 BCE file and remains absent at 300 BCE. Tested main-island points become blank while Sapporo stays Ainu; no exact successor owns the old target geometry. The software endpoint therefore cannot support a conquest, extinction, or single handoff to Yayoi.

Late and Final Jomon are archaeological phase names built from pottery sequences and other dated evidence. They do not identify one government or self-named population. Phase boundaries vary regionally, so this card uses contiguous teaching slices while telling readers that no nationwide calendar changed at midnight.

The official northern Japan site network spans settlements, cemeteries, stone circles, shell middens, and wetlands across changing environments. Those places illuminate long-term sedentary lifeways, but they cannot stand for the entire archipelago. Southern, western, central, and northern sequences require their own evidence and names.

Regional population estimates diverge after the Middle Jomon. Kanto shows a marked contraction while parts of Aomori and Hokkaido follow different paths. Counts depend on site discovery and chronological assumptions, yet their contrast rules out one simple archipelago-wide population crash as the Late Jomon explanation.

Storage studies likewise find differences across time and place rather than one national pattern. Pit volume can suggest planned reserves, but it does not directly count meals, household members, or winter length. Storage is best reconstructed settlement by settlement, alongside plant remains, vessels, and local seasonality.

The atlas calls the record Late Jomon culture but continues it into centuries often labeled Final Jomon. The proposed name makes both phases visible. It also ends around 300 BCE, an approximate convention that leaves room for later Epi-Jomon and regionally delayed transitions.

sections.title: Build homes, graves, and gathering places

items.text: Oyu contains two large stone circles built from river stones, with concentric remains of graves, buildings, storage pits, and other features. Their layout and solar alignment support repeated communal activity. They do not reveal a named architect, ruler, priesthood, or one ritual script used across Japan.

Four stone circles at Isedotai exceed thirty meters in diameter. Nearby pillar buildings, graves, storage pits, ditches, and many ritual objects show a place used in several ways. A missing segment also preserves decisions about construction, although the reason for leaving it open remains uncertain.

Kiusu preserves nine communal earthwork burial circles, eight still visible, with the largest about eighty-three meters across. Excavators estimate roughly three thousand cubic meters of soil were moved. That is excellent evidence for organized labor, but the foreman's name remains stubbornly absent from the dirt.

Omori Katsuyama combines a stone circle with pit-dwelling traces, hearths, dumps, and hundreds of disc-shaped stones. The arrangement faced the winter-solstice sunset across a mountain ridge. Repeated visits and shared observation are plausible; a centralized astronomical office is not required to explain them.

Korekawa was a relatively small Final Jomon settlement with residential areas, graves, refuse, stone features, and earthen mounds. Waterlogged deposits preserved wooden objects and foods. Its compact scale and exceptional preservation demonstrate one community's practices, not a standard village plan imposed across the archipelago.

sections.title: Eat from forests, rivers, shores, and stores

items.text: Official summaries describe chestnuts, walnuts, horse chestnuts, acorns, berries, fish, shellfish, deer, boar, and other resources. Some bitter nuts required soaking and processing. This mixed repertoire joined gathering, plant management, fishing, hunting, and storage; its balance varied strongly by place and season.

A systematic food database finds substantial temporal and regional variation in Jomon plant and animal use. That result matters more than a single menu. It replaces the generic hunter-gatherer label with testable local combinations of cultivated, managed, gathered, hunted, and aquatic resources.

Shell middens preserve repeated harvesting of coastal and river foods, tools, animal remains, and sometimes human burials. Their contents document aquatic expertise and long-term change. They also overrepresent durable shells, so an abundant midden should not make invisible plants, freshwater foods, or meals eaten elsewhere disappear.

Radiography of deer teeth tests hunting seasons rather than merely listing deer bones. Late Jomon patterns can illuminate when animals were taken and whether products moved between coast and interior. The method sharpens seasonal questions while leaving hunters' names, household shares, and exact recipes unknown.

Jaw form and dental evidence also reflect regional dietary histories. Researchers find different chewing environments and only limited movement of certain foods between some communities. Bodies record repeated meals, but no mandible supplies a complete menu or proves that every resident ate equal portions.

sections.title: Make pottery, lacquer, nets, and tools

items.text: Jomon pottery was hand built, often by coiling, then shaped, decorated, and fired without a potter's wheel. Late and Final styles differ by region. A vessel can preserve skilled choices in clay, temper, form, surface, and heat while withholding the maker's name and teaching lineage.

Chemical study of lacquerware identifies multiple layers of Toxicodendron lacquer, drying oil, and pigments such as cinnabar or iron oxide. Preparing surfaces and controlling layered coatings required material knowledge and patience. The analysis documents technique; it does not identify a guild, recipe book, or named inventor.

Net impressions preserved on pottery allow researchers to reconstruct fiber choice, knotting, and mesh near the Jomon-Yayoi transition. An accidental imprint can outlive the net itself. It is wonderfully useful evidence, though the pot still refuses to say who tied the knots or complained about tangles.

A small bone bow nock from Final Jomon Japan shows how perishable hunting equipment survives through durable fittings. It supports bow technology without revealing prey, ownership, or hunting rules in one object. Tool parts become stronger evidence when joined to animal remains, injuries, seasonality, and site context.

Jomon crafts also used stone, bone, antler, shell, wood, bark, fibers, asphalt, and mineral pigments. Asphalt served as an adhesive and repair material, while valued stones traveled far. Technical achievement lay in joining local resources with exchange and practiced knowledge, not in pottery alone.

sections.title: Keep family and social life evidence-sized

items.text: At Yoshigo, isotope modeling suggests breastfeeding and gradual weaning ended around three and a half years on average, with a broad credible range. The sample does not define every family. It offers rare evidence for infant feeding while leaving caregivers, emotions, household composition, and individual circumstances mostly unknown.

Strontium isotopes and ritual tooth-ablation patterns at Yoshigo and Inariyama test whether some adults moved during life. The study evaluates links among mobility, marriage, and social identity rather than declaring one marriage rule. Teeth can narrow possibilities, but they cannot name spouses or describe a wedding.

Intentional tooth removal was a visible, embodied practice with varied individual patterns. Bioarchaeologists examine how it could mark identity and social participation. The evidence supports deliberate modification, while specific initiation ages, kin groups, meanings, and consent experiences remain matters for careful hypothesis rather than confident narration.

Later Jomon dog burials and healed injuries support close relationships between people and hunting dogs. Dogs could help track and hold prey in forested landscapes. Burial shows that some animals received special treatment, but it does not prove every household kept a dog or shared one emotional practice.

A hollow goggle-eyed dogu from Tohoku has a dramatic face and carefully modeled body, but its function remains uncertain. Calling it a mother, deity, toy, patient, or ancestor requires more evidence. The safest family lesson is that a human-shaped object is not automatically a family portrait.

sections.title: Learn skills without inventing schools or texts

items.text: No securely excavated Late or Final Jomon classroom, curriculum, teacher title, or school schedule appears in the reviewed evidence. Children and adults still learned language, landscapes, food processing, craft, and social expectations. Necessary learning does not by itself establish a formal educational institution.

Layered lacquer demanded preparing sap, oils, pigments, surfaces, and drying conditions in the right order. Such work implies observation, practice, correction, and transmitted knowledge. Chemistry can recover materials and sequences, but it cannot tell whether instruction came from relatives, specialists, peers, or several teachers.

Reconstructing nets from pottery impressions reveals repeated choices about fiber, cordage, knots, and mesh. Learners likely practiced those coordinated actions, yet no surviving impression records a lesson plan. A crooked strand may be a mistake, an adjustment, or normal variation, not a prehistoric report card.

The horned-owl dogu from Kanto models hair, clothing, and accessories and retains red color. Those details show learned conventions of making and display, although their meanings remain debated. Its wide eyes can meet ours across millennia; they cannot grade our interpretation or confirm a hairstyle manual.

Written-language sample: none securely attributable to Late or Final Jomon communities, about 1500 to 300 BCE. No original text, script, transliteration, translation, date, or author can be supplied. Established writing in Japan is centuries later, so cord marks and ceramic designs are not promoted into writing.

sections.title: Treat health, medicine, water, and waste honestly

items.text: At Tsukumo, skeletal lesions are consistent with possible scurvy and other nutritional stress, while dental caries increased through time. Diagnosis from ancient bone is probabilistic, and this cemetery cannot represent all regions. The findings reveal real health risks without turning Final Jomon communities into one uniformly sick population.

The consulted sources do not identify a securely attributable Late or Final Jomon medical text, named healer, prescription, hospital, or standardized treatment. People surely responded to illness and injury, but exact remedies remain undocumented. Dogu, pigments, and burial goods cannot be relabeled as medical equipment by visual intuition alone.

Korekawa preserves a watering place used to process horse chestnuts, alongside wetland deposits and settlement refuse. Water was practical infrastructure even without masonry pipes. The feature supports controlled soaking and food preparation, but it does not establish purified drinking water, baths, sewers, or one sanitation code.

Parasite studies report Jomon coprolites in shell middens and discuss dumps outside dwelling areas, but precise toilet arrangements remain uncertain. No secure nationwide latrine plan follows. Human waste can preserve diet and infection evidence while still refusing to provide a neat architectural label for the place of deposition.

Refuse pits, shell middens, and wet deposits show that communities placed waste in recurring locations. Archaeologists can study disposal without assuming modern hygiene categories. The honest sanitation account distinguishes documented dumps from unknown routines for cleaning, privacy, drinking water, bodily waste, and keeping living surfaces usable.

sections.title: Exchange materials and gather for ritual

items.text: Jade, obsidian, amber, asphalt, shells, and finished objects traveled over long distances. Distribution maps demonstrate connections, while the mechanisms may include visiting, gifting, partnership, down-the-line exchange, or mobility. They do not by themselves reveal merchants, prices, taxes, a capital, or one authority controlling routes.

Kamegaoka graves, wetland deposits, lacquerware, jade, figurines, and elaborate pottery make social and ritual activity unusually visible. Wet soil preserved materials lost elsewhere. Rich preservation should prompt comparison, not an automatic claim that this one cemetery governed a northern realm or set ritual rules for every community.

The Oyu circles brought river stones, graves, structures, and ritual objects into planned concentric spaces. Their axes relate to the summer-solstice sunset. This supports repeated gathering and shared seasonal knowledge, while the exact ceremonies, spoken words, participants, and authority structure remain beyond the recovered evidence.

Red pigment, standing stones, entrances, and repeated graves at Kiusu show that burial involved material choices and communal labor. Those traces support remembrance and ceremony without identifying theology. Moving three thousand cubic meters of earth demonstrates coordination; it does not prove a king ordered every basket.

Dogu vary greatly by region and period. Their breakage, deposition, and striking forms invite interpretations involving ritual, bodies, healing, fertility, or protection, but no single explanation is secure everywhere. The goggle-eyed figure is excellent evidence for skilled modeling and terrible evidence for reading a universal creed.

sections.title: Recognize achievements and explain the ending

items.text: Achievements included durable settlements, planned storage, complex food processing, fishing and hunting technologies, lacquer chemistry, fiber work, pottery, exchange, cemeteries, and communal monuments. These accomplishments belonged to many unnamed communities and makers. Credit should follow the evidence across regions rather than collect under an imagined Jomon government.

Early rice farming did not replace every existing practice at once. Research describes interaction between people using Jomon and Yayoi material traditions, with cultivation adopted and adapted regionally. Farming, foraging, fishing, and hunting could overlap while objects, crops, ancestry, and social relationships changed at different speeds.

Archaeobotanical work places crop adoption later in parts of eastern and northern Japan than in the west. Hybrid material practices reveal contact rather than a clean line between separate populations. The atlas's 400 BCE repaint is therefore a cartographic edit, not a synchronized conversion of western households.

Genomic and archaeological models describe a time-transgressive spread of farmers and Japonic languages, while Epi-Jomon lifeways continued in the north. These models concern populations and processes, not an exact successor for this database id. The card leaves predecessor and successor arrays empty to avoid false one-to-one descent.

Around 300 BCE, Late and Final Jomon cease to be the best umbrella for many regional sequences. Communities did not vanish together. Rice cultivation, migration, exchange, intermarriage, and local continuity produced new histories, while northern and island trajectories differed. The ending records transformation, interaction, and changing archaeological labels.

ending.text: Around 300 BCE, Late and Final Jomon stop being the most useful umbrella for many regional sequences, but communities did not disappear together. Rice cultivation and Yayoi material spread discontinuously through migration, exchange, intermarriage, adoption, and local adaptation. Eastern and northern transitions often came later, while Epi-Jomon histories continued in Hokkaido and other island trajectories remained distinct. The atlas transfers western probes to Yayoi at 400 BCE, retains an eastern and northern target polygon, then leaves tested main-island points blank at 323 BCE. Neither software seam dates a single historical fall. People, ancestry, fishing, hunting, plant knowledge, craft, routes, and places continued as archaeological labels changed.
